claim: SNX6 is a ubiquitously expressed PX-BAR protein that plays important roles in retromer-mediated retrograde vesicular transport from endosomes.
source: SNX6 is a ubiquitously expressed PX-BAR protein that plays important roles in retromer-mediated retrograde vesicular transport from endosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: CNS-specific Snx6 knockout mice exhibit deficits in spatial learning and memory.
source: Here we report that CNS-specific Snx6 knockout mice exhibit deficits in spatial learning and memory, accompanied with loss of spines from distal dendrites of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from Morris water maze tests shown in Figure 2J-M.

claim: CNS-specific Snx6 knockout mice show loss of spines from distal dendrites of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: Here we report that CNS-specific Snx6 knockout mice exhibit deficits in spatial learning and memory, accompanied with loss of spines from distal dendrites of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 3C-D showing decreased spine density in distal apical dendrites of CA1 neurons.

claim: SNX6 interacts with Homer1b/c, a postsynaptic scaffold protein crucial for the synaptic distribution of other postsynaptic density (PSD) proteins and structural integrity of dendritic spines.
source: SNX6 interacts with Homer1b/c, a postsynaptic scaffold protein crucial for the synaptic distribution of other postsynaptic density (PSD) proteins and structural integrity of dendritic spines.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry, co-immunoprecipitation, and in vitro binding assays shown in Figure 4C-H.

claim: SNX6 functions independently of retromer to regulate distribution of Homer1b/c in the dendritic shaft.
source: We show that SNX6 functions independently of retromer to regulate distribution of Homer1b/c in the dendritic shaft.
evidence: This is supported by VPS35 knockdown experiments and live imaging data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Homer1b/c translocates from shaft to spines by protein diffusion, which does not require SNX6.
source: We also find that Homer1b/c translocates from shaft to spines by protein diffusion, which does not require SNX6.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP analysis shown in Figure 8C-D and live imaging data.

claim: Ablation of SNX6 causes reduced distribution of Homer1b/c in distal dendrites.
source: Ablation of SNX6 causes reduced distribution of Homer1b/c in distal dendrites, decrease in surface levels of AMPAR and impaired AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5A-F.

claim: Ablation of SNX6 causes decrease in surface levels of AMPAR.
source: Ablation of SNX6 causes reduced distribution of Homer1b/c in distal dendrites, decrease in surface levels of AMPAR and impaired AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is supported by surface staining and biotinylation assays shown in Figure 9G-K.

claim: Ablation of SNX6 causes impaired AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission.
source: Ablation of SNX6 causes reduced distribution of Homer1b/c in distal dendrites, decrease in surface levels of AMPAR and impaired AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 9B.

claim: SNX6 was ubiquitously expressed in mouse tissues.
source: Immunoblotting analysis of tissue lysates indicated that SNX6 was ubiquitously expressed in mouse (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In mouse brain, SNX6 was expressed in both the somatodendritic area and processes of neurons in the cortex and the hippocampal formation.
source: In mouse brain, SNX6 was expressed in both the somatodendritic area and processes of neurons in the cortex and the hippocampal formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: SNX6 was primarily located in dendrites.
source: Quantitative analysis of fluorescence signal intensity revealed that SNX6 was primarily located in dendrites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: SNX6 partially colocalized with PSD95, a postsynaptic marker in dendritic spines but not synaptophysin, a presynaptic marker.
source: Moreover, SNX6 partially colocalized with PSD95, a postsynaptic marker in dendritic spines but not synaptophysin, a presynaptic marker (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: CNS-Snx6 KO mice were born with the expected Mendelian ratio and appeared indistinguishable from wild-type littermates.
source: CNS-Snx6 KO mice were born with the expected Mendelian ratio and appeared indistinguishable from wild-type littermates.
evidence: This is an observational statement about the mice.

claim: The brain size of CNS-Snx6 KO mice was comparable with that of wild-type.
source: Their brain size was comparable with that of wild-type (Figure 1E), and no gross abnormalities in the structure of the cortex, hippocampus and cerebellum were observed by histological examination (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by brain weight measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: No gross abnormalities in the structure of the cortex, hippocampus and cerebellum were observed in CNS-Snx6 KO mice by histological examination.
source: Their brain size was comparable with that of wild-type (Figure 1E), and no gross abnormalities in the structure of the cortex, hippocampus and cerebellum were observed by histological examination (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by Nissl staining shown in Figure 1F.

claim: No change in locomotor activity was detected in CNS-Snx6 KO mice by rotarod and open field assays.
source: No change in locomotor activity was detected by rotarod and open field assays (Figure 2A,B), and the mood levels of CNS-Snx6 KO were also similar to that of wild-type mice in elevated plus maze, tail suspension and forced swimming tests (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The mood levels of CNS-Snx6 KO mice were similar to that of wild-type mice in elevated plus maze, tail suspension and forced swimming tests.
source: No change in locomotor activity was detected by rotarod and open field assays (Figure 2A,B), and the mood levels of CNS-Snx6 KO were also similar to that of wild-type mice in elevated plus maze, tail suspension and forced swimming tests (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: CNS-Snx6 KO mice showed no abnormality in sociability and social novelty in the Three-Chamber test.
source: In the Three-Chamber test, the CNS-Snx6 KO mice showed no abnormality in sociability and social novelty (Figure 2F), nor did they display repetitive behaviors (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CNS-Snx6 KO mice did not display repetitive behaviors.
source: In the Three-Chamber test, the CNS-Snx6 KO mice showed no abnormality in sociability and social novelty (Figure 2F), nor did they display repetitive behaviors (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Nestin-Cre; Snx6fl/fl mice performed as well as their littermates in Y maze and shuttle box.
source: Although Nestin-Cre; Snx6fl/fl mice performed as well as their littermates in Y maze and shuttle box (Figure 2H,I), in the Morris water maze test, they were significantly retarded in spatial learning using latency traveled to reach the hidden platform as measures (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: In the Morris water maze test, Nestin-Cre; Snx6fl/fl mice were significantly retarded in spatial learning using latency traveled to reach the hidden platform as measures.
source: Although Nestin-Cre; Snx6fl/fl mice performed as well as their littermates in Y maze and shuttle box (Figure 2H,I), in the Morris water maze test, they were significantly retarded in spatial learning using latency traveled to reach the hidden platform as measures (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: A probe trial showed that Nestin-Cre; Snx6fl/fl mice were severely impaired in spatial memory.
source: A probe trial showed that they were also severely impaired in spatial memory (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Nestin-Cre; Snx6fl/fl mice exhibited deficits in memory recall.
source: Moreover, these mice exhibited deficits in memory recall (Figure 2L,M).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2L-M.

claim: The hippocampal region participates in the processes of the encoding, storage, consolidation and retrieval of spatial memory.
source: As the hippocampal region participates in the processes of the encoding, storage, consolidation and retrieval of spatial memory (Riedel et al., 1999), the behavioral phenotypes suggest that ablation of SNX6 affects synaptic function of hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Riedel et al., 1999.

claim: The behavioral phenotypes suggest that ablation of SNX6 affects synaptic function of hippocampal neurons.
source: As the hippocampal region participates in the processes of the encoding, storage, consolidation and retrieval of spatial memory (Riedel et al., 1999), the behavioral phenotypes suggest that ablation of SNX6 affects synaptic function of hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data and knowledge about hippocampal function.

claim: There was a decrease in the spine density of the distal portion of apical dendrites of Snx6-/- CA1 neurons.
source: Quantitative analysis showed that, although spine morphology did not change in either CA1 or CA3 pyramidal cells (Figure 3C–F), there was a decrease in the spine density of the distal portion of apical dendrites of Snx6-/- CA1 neurons (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Spine morphology did not change in either CA1 or CA3 pyramidal cells of Snx6-/- mice.
source: Quantitative analysis showed that, although spine morphology did not change in either CA1 or CA3 pyramidal cells (Figure 3C–F), there was a decrease in the spine density of the distal portion of apical dendrites of Snx6-/- CA1 neurons (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: No change in spine density was detected in Snx6-/- CA3 neurons.
source: In contrast, no change in spine density was detected in Snx6-/- CA3 neurons (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Ultrastructural analysis revealed a decrease in the number of asymmetric/excitatory synapses in the CA1, but not in the CA3 region of Nestin-Cre; Snx6fl/fl mouse brain.
source: Consistently, ultrastructural analysis revealed a decrease in the number of asymmetric/excitatory synapses in the CA1, but not in the CA3 region of Nestin-Cre; Snx6fl/fl mouse brain (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: SNX6 is required for spine morphogenesis and/or maintenance of distal apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Together, these data indicate that SNX6 is required for spine morphogenesis and/or maintenance of distal apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spine density and synapse number data.

claim: The majority of SNX6 signals colocalized with EEA1 and Rab5B, the early endosome markers.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed that the majority of SNX6 signals colocalized with EEA1 and Rab5B, the early endosome markers (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: SNX6 partially colocalized with the late endosome marker Rab7 and Rab4, marker for the fast recycling pathway, though to a lesser extent, but not Rab11 recycling endosomes.
source: SNX6 also partially colocalized with the late endosome marker Rab7 and Rab4, marker for the fast recycling pathway, though to a lesser extent, but not Rab11 recycling endosomes (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: SNX6 signals did not colocalize with Golgin97, a TGN resident protein.
source: Intriguingly, although SNX6 signals did not colocalize with Golgin97, a TGN resident protein, they overlapped partially with TGN46 (Figure 4A,B), a protein involved in membrane traffic to and from the TGN (Ponnambalam et al., 1996), suggesting that SNX6 associates with endosomes and transport carriers in the dendrite.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: SNX6 signals overlapped partially with TGN46, a protein involved in membrane traffic to and from the TGN.
source: Intriguingly, although SNX6 signals did not colocalize with Golgin97, a TGN resident protein, they overlapped partially with TGN46 (Figure 4A,B), a protein involved in membrane traffic to and from the TGN (Ponnambalam et al., 1996), suggesting that SNX6 associates with endosomes and transport carriers in the dendrite.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4A-B and a citation to Ponnambalam et al., 1996.

claim: SNX6 associates with endosomes and transport carriers in the dendrite.
source: Intriguingly, although SNX6 signals did not colocalize with Golgin97, a TGN resident protein, they overlapped partially with TGN46 (Figure 4A,B), a protein involved in membrane traffic to and from the TGN (Ponnambalam et al., 1996), suggesting that SNX6 associates with endosomes and transport carriers in the dendrite.
evidence: This is an inference based on the colocalization data.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis revealed six matching peptides with 24% sequence coverage corresponding to Homer1b/c from SNX6-N pull down from mouse brain lysates.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis revealed six matching peptides with 24% sequence coverage corresponding to Homer1b/c, a postsynaptic scaffold protein (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Immunoblotting analysis verified that Homer1b/c, not Homer1a, was pulled down by the N-terminus of SNX6 but not SNX1.
source: Immunoblotting analysis verified that Homer1b/c, not Homer1a, the shorter isoform encoded by the Homer1 gene, was pulled down by the N-terminus of SNX6 but not SNX1 (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: In vitro binding assays showed that SNX6-N interacted directly with the coiled-coil domain of Homer1b/c.
source: Moreover, in vitro binding assays showed that SNX6-N interacted directly with the coiled-coil domain of Homer1b/c (Figure 4F), which is not present in Homer1a.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Neither Homer2b nor Homer3, the longer isoforms of other Homer family members, interacted with SNX6-N.
source: In contrast, neither Homer2b nor Homer3, the longer isoforms of other Homer family members, interacted with SNX6-N (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: mEmerald-Homer1c co-immunoprecipitated with Flag-tagged SNX6 in transiently transfected HEK293T cells.
source: Further, mEmerald-Homer1c co-immunoprecipitated with Flag-tagged SNX6 in transiently transfected HEK293T cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Reciprocal co-immunoprecipitations of endogenous proteins from mouse brain lysates verified that SNX6 and Homer1b/c interact with each other.
source: Consistently, reciprocal co-immunoprecipitations of endogenous proteins from mouse brain lysates verified that SNX6 and Homer1b/c interact with each other (Figure 4I, left and center panels).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Immunoisolation of SNX6-positive vesicles from membrane fractions of mouse brain lysates detected Homer1b/c together with p150Glued and dynein intermediate chain (DIC), subunits of the dynein−dynactin complex.
source: Moreover, immunoisolation of SNX6-positive vesicles from membrane fractions of mouse brain lysates detected Homer1b/c together with p150Glued and dynein intermediate chain (DIC), subunits of the dynein−dynactin complex (Figure 4I, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by immunoisolation data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Neither Homer1a nor subunits of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) were detected on SNX6-positive vesicles.
source: In contrast, neither Homer1a nor subunits of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) were detected on SNX6-positive vesicles (Figure 4I, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by immunoisolation data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: In dendrites, Homer1b/c colocalized with SNX6 on vesicular structures.
source: In dendrites, Homer1b/c not only colocalized with SNX6 on vesicular structures (Figure 4J,K), but also colocalized with EEA1 (Figure 4L,M).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4J-K.

claim: Homer1b/c colocalized with EEA1 in dendrites.
source: In dendrites, Homer1b/c not only colocalized with SNX6 on vesicular structures (Figure 4J,K), but also colocalized with EEA1 (Figure 4L,M).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4L-M.

claim: Wide-field microscopy with deconvolution and superresolution fluorescence microscopy revealed colocalization of EEA1, Homer1b/c and SNX6 in dendrites.
source: Both wide-field microscopy with deconvolution and superresolution fluorescence microscopy revealed colocalization of EEA1, Homer1b/c and SNX6 in dendrites (Figure 4N, Table 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Video 1), indicating that SNX6 associates with Homer1b/c on endosomes.
evidence: This is supported by superresolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4N and Table 1.

claim: SNX6 associates with Homer1b/c on endosomes.
source: Both wide-field microscopy with deconvolution and superresolution fluorescence microscopy revealed colocalization of EEA1, Homer1b/c and SNX6 in dendrites (Figure 4N, Table 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Video 1), indicating that SNX6 associates with Homer1b/c on endosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the colocalization data.

claim: There was a decrease in the number of Homer1b/c puncta in dendritic segments (30–120 μm from the cell body) of Snx6-/- neurons as compared with that of Snx6+/+.
source: Indeed, although no change in the protein levels of Homer1b/c was detected in the hippocampi of Nestin-Cre; Snx6fl/fl mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), quantitative analysis revealed not only a decrease in the number of Homer1b/c puncta in dendritic segments (30–120 μm from the cell body) of Snx6-/- neurons as compared with that of Snx6+/+, but also a significant reduction in the fluorescence intensity of Homer1b/c puncta in spines (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the fluorescence intensity of Homer1b/c puncta in spines of Snx6-/- neurons.
source: Indeed, although no change in the protein levels of Homer1b/c was detected in the hippocampi of Nestin-Cre; Snx6fl/fl mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), quantitative analysis revealed not only a decrease in the number of Homer1b/c puncta in dendritic segments (30–120 μm from the cell body) of Snx6-/- neurons as compared with that of Snx6+/+, but also a significant reduction in the fluorescence intensity of Homer1b/c puncta in spines (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Overexpression of EGFP-SNX6 rescued both puncta number and spine distribution of Homer1b/c in Snx6-/- neurons.
source: Overexpression of EGFP-SNX6 rescued both puncta number and spine distribution of Homer1b/c in Snx6-/- neurons (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Neither the number nor the fluorescence intensity of PSD95 puncta was significantly affected in Snx6-/- neurons.
source: In contrast, neither the number nor the fluorescence intensity of PSD95 puncta was significantly affected in Snx6-/- neurons (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Quantification of the Homer1b/c signal intensity over distance from the cell body revealed a decrease in both shaft and spines of the distal dendrites and concurrent accumulation in the soma of Snx6-/- neurons, which was rescued by mCherry-SNX6.
source: Further, quantification of the Homer1b/c signal intensity over distance from the cell body revealed a decrease in both shaft and spines of the distal dendrites and concurrent accumulation in the soma of Snx6-/- neurons, which was rescued by mCherry-SNX6 (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: SNX6 is required for Homer1b/c distribution in distal dendrites.
source: Together these data indicate that SNX6 is required for Homer1b/c distribution in distal dendrites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Homer1b/c distribution data.

claim: The spine density of Snx6-/- neurons was lower than that of Snx6+/+ in dissociated cultures.
source: Consistent with the in vivo data, the spine density of Snx6-/- neurons was lower than that of Snx6+/+ in dissociated cultures (Figure 5G,H, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: Overexpression of EGFP-SNX6 or mEmerald-Homer1c but not a Homer1c fragment that is truncated of its mGluR1/5-binding EVH1 domain (Homer1c-C) restored the spine density of Snx6-/- neurons.
source: Overexpression of EGFP-SNX6 or mEmerald-Homer1c but not a Homer1c fragment that is truncated of its mGluR1/5-binding EVH1 domain (Homer1c-C) (Shiraishi-Yamaguchi and Furuichi, 2007) restored the spine density of Snx6-/- neurons (Figure 5G,H), indicating that SNX6-dependent dendritic distribution of Homer1b/c contributes to spine formation/stabilization, and that the cellular function of Homer1b/c as postsynaptic scaffold protein is required to restore the number of spines.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5G-H and a citation to Shiraishi-Yamaguchi and Furuichi, 2007.

claim: SNX6-dependent dendritic distribution of Homer1b/c contributes to spine formation/stabilization.
source: Overexpression of EGFP-SNX6 or mEmerald-Homer1c but not a Homer1c fragment that is truncated of its mGluR1/5-binding EVH1 domain (Homer1c-C) (Shiraishi-Yamaguchi and Furuichi, 2007) restored the spine density of Snx6-/- neurons (Figure 5G,H), indicating that SNX6-dependent dendritic distribution of Homer1b/c contributes to spine formation/stabilization, and that the cellular function of Homer1b/c as postsynaptic scaffold protein is required to restore the number of spines.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments.

claim: The cellular function of Homer1b/c as postsynaptic scaffold protein is required to restore the number of spines.
source: Overexpression of EGFP-SNX6 or mEmerald-Homer1c but not a Homer1c fragment that is truncated of its mGluR1/5-binding EVH1 domain (Homer1c-C) (Shiraishi-Yamaguchi and Furuichi, 2007) restored the spine density of Snx6-/- neurons (Figure 5G,H), indicating that SNX6-dependent dendritic distribution of Homer1b/c contributes to spine formation/stabilization, and that the cellular function of Homer1b/c as postsynaptic scaffold protein is required to restore the number of spines.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments.

claim: Movement of SNX6-, Homer1c-double positive puncta was observed in the shaft of both proximal and distal dendrites.
source: Indeed, we observed movement of SNX6-, Homer1c-double positive puncta in the shaft of both proximal and distal dendrites (Figure 6A–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B, Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6A-C and Videos 2-3.

claim: The majority (~90%) of Homer1c puncta (1022 out of 1128 puncta from 31 neurons) were stationary.
source: Quantitative analysis revealed that, similar to mobility characteristics of PSD95 clusters in dendrites (Gerrow et al., 2006), the majority (~90%) of Homer1c puncta (1022 out of 1128 puncta from 31 neurons) were stationary.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data and a citation to Gerrow et al., 2006.

claim: The majority of motile SNX6-, Homer1c-positive puncta were smaller than 0.3 μm2 in size (<600 nm in apparent diameter), whereas most of the immotile ones were larger.
source: Of note, the majority of motile SNX6-, Homer1c-positive puncta were smaller than 0.3 μm2 in size (<600 nm in apparent diameter), whereas most of the immotile ones were larger (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that the moving structures were vesicles rather than large protein aggregates.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The moving structures were vesicles rather than large protein aggregates.
source: Of note, the majority of motile SNX6-, Homer1c-positive puncta were smaller than 0.3 μm2 in size (<600 nm in apparent diameter), whereas most of the immotile ones were larger (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that the moving structures were vesicles rather than large protein aggregates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the size distribution data.

claim: The SNX6-, Homer1c-positive puncta moved bidirectionally in the dendritic shaft, with the mean velocity of 0.416 ± 0.037 μm/s, over distances ranging from 2.026 to 18.324 μm.
source: The SNX6-, Homer1c-positive puncta moved bidirectionally in the dendritic shaft, with the mean velocity of 0.416 ± 0.037 μm/s, over distances ranging from 2.026 to 18.324 μm (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D-F.

claim: Movement of SNX6-, Homer1b-double positive puncta in the dendritic shaft was observed by live imaging.
source: Movement of SNX6-, Homer1b-double positive puncta in the dendritic shaft was also observed by live imaging (Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Video 4.

claim: No comovement of SNX6- and GluN1-positive vesicles in dendrite was observed in neurons overexpressing EGFP fusion of the GluN1 subunit of NMDAR.
source: In contrast, in neurons overexpressing EGFP fusion of the GluN1 subunit of NMDAR, no comovement of SNX6- and GluN1-positive vesicles in dendrite was observed (Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Video 5.

claim: Compared with wild-type, there was a dramatic decrease in the fraction of motile Homer1c fluorescent puncta in Snx6-/- neurons.
source: Moreover, we performed live imaging of mEmerald-Homer1c in Snx6-/- neurons and found that compared with wild-type, there was a dramatic decrease in the fraction of motile Homer1c fluorescent puncta (29 motile puncta out of 311 from 10 Snx6+/+ neurons vs. 10 out of 1217 from 40 Snx6-/- neurons).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data.

claim: Superresolution microscopy analysis revealed that a significant fraction of both p150Glued and DIC colocalized with SNX6 and Homer1b/c on vesicular structures.
source: Consistent with the immunoisolation data (Figure 4I), superresolution microscopy analysis revealed that a significant fraction of both p150Glued and DIC colocalized with SNX6 and Homer1b/c on vesicular structures (Figure 6D, Table 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Videos 10 and 11).
evidence: This is supported by superresolution microscopy data shown in Figure 6D and Table 1.

claim: Transient treatment of neurons with Ciliobrevin D, an inhibitor of dynein activity, caused a decrease in both shaft and synaptic distribution of Homer1b/c in distal dendrites.
source: Because dynein is essential for cell viability, we transiently treated neurons with Ciliobrevin D, an inhibitor of dynein activity (Firestone et al., 2012), and detected a decrease in both shaft and synaptic distribution of Homer1b/c in distal dendrites (Figure 6E–H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6E-H and a citation to Firestone et al., 2012.

claim: Overexpression of p150Glued-N, a dominant negative mutant that disrupts the interaction between SNX6 and dynactin, caused a decrease in Homer1b/c signals in distal dendrites and concurrent increase in the soma.
source: Further, overexpression of p150Glued-N, a dominant negative mutant that disrupts the interaction between SNX6 and dynactin (Hong et al., 2009), also caused a decrease in Homer1b/c signals in distal dendrites and concurrent increase in the soma (Figure 6I,J), indicating a role for dynein−dynactin in the dendritic distribution of Homer1b/c.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6I-J and a citation to Hong et al., 2009.

claim: Dynein−dynactin plays a role in the dendritic distribution of Homer1b/c.
source: Further, overexpression of p150Glued-N, a dominant negative mutant that disrupts the interaction between SNX6 and dynactin (Hong et al., 2009), also caused a decrease in Homer1b/c signals in distal dendrites and concurrent increase in the soma (Figure 6I,J), indicating a role for dynein−dynactin in the dendritic distribution of Homer1b/c.
evidence: This is an inference based on the p150Glued-N overexpression data.

claim: Western blotting of vesicles immunoisolated with antibodies to both p150Glued and DIC detected Homer1b/c signals in wild-type but not CNS-SNX6 KO mice.
source: Although antibodies to Homer1b/c failed to isolate Homer1b/c-positive vesicles from membrane fractions of mouse brain lysates, western blotting of vesicles immunoisolated with antibodies to both p150Glued and DIC detected Homer1b/c signals in wild-type but not CNS-SNX6 KO mice (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is supported by immunoisolation data shown in Figure 6K.

claim: There was a decrease in colocalization of Homer1b/c with p150Glued and DIC, but not with EEA1, in Snx6-/- neurons.
source: Moreover, we performed immunostaining and colocalization analysis of Homer1b/c on Snx6+/+ and Snx6-/- neurons. Quantitative analysis of confocal images showed that there was a decrease in colocalization of Homer1b/c with p150Glued and DIC, but not with EEA1, in Snx6-/- neurons (Figure 6L,M).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 6L-M.

claim: SNX6 mediates dynein−dynactin-driven transport of a fraction of Homer1b/c molecules in the dendritic shaft.
source: Together, these data suggest that SNX6 mediates dynein−dynactin-driven transport of a fraction of Homer1b/c molecules in the dendritic shaft.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunoisolation and colocalization data.

claim: No SNX6/Homer1b/c signals were detected on motile PSD95 clusters.
source: To determine whether Homer1b/c shares the same trafficking pathway with PSD95, we performed live imaging of neurons expressing PSD95-RFP and determined association of SNX6 and Homer1b/c with motile PSD95 clusters by retrospective immunofluorescence staining. No SNX6/Homer1b/c signals were detected on motile PSD95 clusters (seven motile PSD95 puncta from five cells, Figure 7A and Video 12), indicating that Homer1b/c is not cotransported with PSD95.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging and retrospective staining data shown in Figure 7A and Video 12.

claim: Homer1b/c is not cotransported with PSD95.
source: To determine whether Homer1b/c shares the same trafficking pathway with PSD95, we performed live imaging of neurons expressing PSD95-RFP and determined association of SNX6 and Homer1b/c with motile PSD95 clusters by retrospective immunofluorescence staining. No SNX6/Homer1b/c signals were detected on motile PSD95 clusters (seven motile PSD95 puncta from five cells, Figure 7A and Video 12), indicating that Homer1b/c is not cotransported with PSD95.
evidence: This is an inference based on the live imaging data.

claim: Expression of PKD-KD did not affect either dendritic distribution or spine localization of Homer1b/c.
source: To address this question, we transfected neurons with plasmid overexpressing a kinase-dead version of protein kinase D1 (PKD1-K618N, or PKD-KD), which blocks secretory trafficking by preventing fission of transport carriers from the TGN (Liljedahl et al., 2001). Expression of PKD-KD did not affect either dendritic distribution or spine localization of Homer1b/c (Figure 7B–E), indicating that its dendritic trafficking and synaptic delivery does not rely on the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7B-E and a citation to Liljedahl et al., 2001.

claim: Homer1b/c dendritic trafficking and synaptic delivery does not rely on the secretory pathway.
source: To address this question, we transfected neurons with plasmid overexpressing a kinase-dead version of protein kinase D1 (PKD1-K618N, or PKD-KD), which blocks secretory trafficking by preventing fission of transport carriers from the TGN (Liljedahl et al., 2001). Expression of PKD-KD did not affect either dendritic distribution or spine localization of Homer1b/c (Figure 7B–E), indicating that its dendritic trafficking and synaptic delivery does not rely on the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PKD-KD overexpression data.

claim: In live imaging experiments using mEmerald-Homer1c, entry of Homer1c puncta into spines was not detected in either wild-type or Snx6 KO neurons.
source: First, we determined whether or not shaft-localized Homer1b/c puncta enter spines. In our live imaging experiments using mEmerald-Homer1c, we did not detect entry of Homer1c puncta into spines in either wild-type or Snx6 KO neurons.
evidence: This is based on live imaging observations.

claim: Under the experimental condition used, most motile fluorescent puncta moved in shaft, only one event of Homer1c particle entry into spine was observed.
source: We also imaged dendritic segments of neurons expressing mCherry-Homer1c (Snx6+/+: 30 cells, 50 dendritic segments, 791 spines; Snx6-/-: 30 cells, 50 dendritic segments, 547 spines). Under the experimental condition we used, most motile fluorescent puncta moved in shaft (Figure 8A and Video 13), only one event of Homer1c particle entry into spine was observed (Video 14).
evidence: This is based on live imaging observations shown in Figure 8A and Videos 13-14.

claim: Although both total and spine Homer1b/c signals decreased in distal dendrites, its spine:shaft ratio remained constant throughout the dendrite and did not change in Snx6-/- neurons.
source: Moreover, we reasoned that if delivery of Homer1b/c from shaft to spines requires SNX6, there would be a decrease in spine distribution of Homer1b/c signals in dendrites of Snx6 KO neurons. Quantitative analysis showed that, although both total and spine Homer1b/c signals decreased in distal dendrites (Figure 5F), its spine:shaft ratio remained constant throughout the dendrite and did not change in Snx6-/- neurons (Figure 8B), indicating that in steady-state neurons, SNX6 is not involved in local trafficking of Homer1b/c from shaft to spines.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In steady-state neurons, SNX6 is not involved in local trafficking of Homer1b/c from shaft to spines.
source: Moreover, we reasoned that if delivery of Homer1b/c from shaft to spines requires SNX6, there would be a decrease in spine distribution of Homer1b/c signals in dendrites of Snx6 KO neurons. Quantitative analysis showed that, although both total and spine Homer1b/c signals decreased in distal dendrites (Figure 5F), its spine:shaft ratio remained constant throughout the dendrite and did not change in Snx6-/- neurons (Figure 8B), indicating that in steady-state neurons, SNX6 is not involved in local trafficking of Homer1b/c from shaft to spines.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spine:shaft ratio data.

claim: Following full synapse photobleaching of fluorescent signals, 7 ~ 9 % of recovery after 10 s was observed in both wild-type and Snx6 KO neurons.
source: Consistent with previous findings on Homer1c turnover rates measured by FRAP using EGFP-Homer1c (Kuriu et al., 2006), following full synapse photobleaching of fluorescent signals, 7 ~ 9 % of recovery after 10 s was observed in both wild-type and Snx6 KO neurons (8.09 ± 0.91% in Snx6+/+ and 8.14 ± 0.73% in Snx6-/- neurons, Figure 8C,D), indicating that although the fraction of fast fluorescence recovery in spines attributable to entry of soluble cytosolic proteins (Blanpied et al., 2008; Kerr and Blanpied, 2012; Kuriu et al., 2006) is minor, diffusion of Homer1c protein molecules into spines does not require SNX6.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 8C-D and citations to Kuriu et al., 2006; Blanpied et al., 2008; Kerr and Blanpied, 2012.

claim: Diffusion of Homer1c protein molecules into spines does not require SNX6.
source: Consistent with previous findings on Homer1c turnover rates measured by FRAP using EGFP-Homer1c (Kuriu et al., 2006), following full synapse photobleaching of fluorescent signals, 7 ~ 9 % of recovery after 10 s was observed in both wild-type and Snx6 KO neurons (8.09 ± 0.91% in Snx6+/+ and 8.14 ± 0.73% in Snx6-/- neurons, Figure 8C,D), indicating that although the fraction of fast fluorescence recovery in spines attributable to entry of soluble cytosolic proteins (Blanpied et al., 2008; Kerr and Blanpied, 2012; Kuriu et al., 2006) is minor, diffusion of Homer1c protein molecules into spines does not require SNX6.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRAP data.

claim: After 10 min, about half of Homer1c fluorescence was recovered in both wild-type and Snx6 KO neurons with similar recovery half-time.
source: After 10 min, about half of Homer1c fluorescence was recovered in both wild-type and Snx6 KO neurons with similar recovery half-time (Recovery level Rfinal = 54.55 ± 4.03%, τ1/2 = 108.4 ± 9.4 s in Snx6+/+ and Rfinal = 52.63 ± 3.53%, τ1/2 = 107.2 ± 13.1 s in Snx6-/-, Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 8C-D.

claim: The dynamic turnover of Homer1c in spines is not affected by ablation of SNX6.
source: Further, similar results were obtained by fitting a single-exponential recovery curve to the average recovery time trace (τ1/2 = 117.6 ± 11.3 s, Rfinal = 51.63 ± 0.86% in Snx6+/+ and τ1/2 = 108.9 ± 9.1 s, Rfinal = 48.57 ± 0.73% in Snx6-/-). These results are in good agreement with previous findings that there are immobile and mobile fractions of Homer1c in spines (Kuriu et al., 2006) and indicate that the dynamic turnover of Homer1c in spines is not affected by ablation of SNX6.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRAP data and a citation to Kuriu et al., 2006.

claim: In steady-state neurons, neither SNX6 nor vesicular transport is required for recruitment of Homer1b/c from shaft to spines.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that in steady-state neurons, neither SNX6 nor vesicular transport is required for recruitment of Homer1b/c from shaft to spines, and that synaptic Homer1b/c exchanges with the soluble protein pool that enters the spine by diffusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the live imaging and FRAP data.

claim: Synaptic Homer1b/c exchanges with the soluble protein pool that enters the spine by diffusion.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that in steady-state neurons, neither SNX6 nor vesicular transport is required for recruitment of Homer1b/c from shaft to spines, and that synaptic Homer1b/c exchanges with the soluble protein pool that enters the spine by diffusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP data.

claim: AMPAR-mediated eEPSCs were significantly impaired by about 50% with ablation of SNX6.
source: By simultaneous recording the evoked EPSCs (eEPSCs) on infected and adjacent uninfected CA1 pyramidal neurons, we found that AMPAR-mediated eEPSCs were significantly impaired by about 50% with ablation of SNX6 (Figure 9B), whereas NMDAR-mediated eEPSCs and the pair-pulse ratio of AMPAR eEPSCs were unaffected (Figure 9C,D), indicating that the impairment of AMPAR eEPSCs is due to decrease in the number of AMPARs in the postsynaptic membrane but not reduction of presynaptic glutamate release.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: NMDAR-mediated eEPSCs and the pair-pulse ratio of AMPAR eEPSCs were unaffected by ablation of SNX6.
source: By simultaneous recording the evoked EPSCs (eEPSCs) on infected and adjacent uninfected CA1 pyramidal neurons, we found that AMPAR-mediated eEPSCs were significantly impaired by about 50% with ablation of SNX6 (Figure 9B), whereas NMDAR-mediated eEPSCs and the pair-pulse ratio of AMPAR eEPSCs were unaffected (Figure 9C,D), indicating that the impairment of AMPAR eEPSCs is due to decrease in the number of AMPARs in the postsynaptic membrane but not reduction of presynaptic glutamate release.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9C-D.

claim: The impairment of AMPAR eEPSCs is due to decrease in the number of AMPARs in the postsynaptic membrane but not reduction of presynaptic glutamate release.
source: By simultaneous recording the evoked EPSCs (eEPSCs) on infected and adjacent uninfected CA1 pyramidal neurons, we found that AMPAR-mediated eEPSCs were significantly impaired by about 50% with ablation of SNX6 (Figure 9B), whereas NMDAR-mediated eEPSCs and the pair-pulse ratio of AMPAR eEPSCs were unaffected (Figure 9C,D), indicating that the impairment of AMPAR eEPSCs is due to decrease in the number of AMPARs in the postsynaptic membrane but not reduction of presynaptic glutamate release.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: No change in surface expression of the GluN2B subunit of NMDAR was detected in Snx6-/- neurons.
source: Indeed, no change in surface expression of the GluN2B subunit of NMDAR was detected in Snx6-/- neurons by immunostaining and quantitative analysis (Figure 9E,F).
evidence: This is supported by surface staining data shown in Figure 9E-F.

claim: There was a decrease in the surface expression of GluA1 and GluA2, components of AMPAR, in Snx6-/- neurons, which was fully rescued by overexpressing SNX6 or Homer1c.
source: In contrast, there was a decrease in the surface expression of GluA1 and GluA2, components of AMPAR, which was fully rescued by overexpressing SNX6 or Homer1c (Figure 9G–J).
evidence: This is supported by surface staining and biotinylation data shown in Figure 9G-K.

claim: There was an increase in surface levels of mGluR5 in Snx6-/- neurons.
source: The longer isoforms of Homer inhibit not only trafficking to synaptic membrane but also constitutive activities of mGluR1/5 (Ango et al., 2001, 2002 ; Roche et al., 1999). mGluR activation down-regulates surface expression of AMPAR by increasing its endocytosis rate (Snyder et al., 2001). Indeed, there was an increase in surface levels of mGluR5 in Snx6-/- neurons (Figure 9K, Figure 9—figure supplements 2 and 3), which was restored by overexpression of SNX6 or Homer1c but not Homer1c-C (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by surface staining and biotinylation data shown in Figure 9K and Figure 9—figure supplements 2-3, and citations to Ango et al., 2001, 2002; Roche et al., 1999; Snyder et al., 2001.

claim: Ratiometric analysis of internalized and surface AMPAR detected an increase in the rate of AMPAR endocytosis in Snx6-/- neurons.
source: Moreover, ratiometric analysis of internalized and surface AMPAR detected an increase in the rate of AMPAR endocytosis in Snx6-/- neurons ( Figure 9L,M ).
evidence: This is supported by antibody uptake assay data shown in Figure 9L-M.

claim: Inhibition of mGluRs rescued surface expression of AMPAR in Snx6-/- neurons.
source: To test the possibility that loss of Homer1b/c leads to decrease in surface AMPAR via increased surface levels and/or constitutive activation of mGluRs, we treated neurons with inverse agonists for mGluR1/5 and determined surface levels of GluA1 and GluA2 by immunostaining. Quantitative analysis indicated that inhibition of mGluRs did rescue surface expression of AMPAR in Snx6-/- neurons (Figure 9N–Q).
evidence: This is supported by surface staining data shown in Figure 9N-Q.

claim: Dendritic loss of Homer1b/c caused by ablation of SNX6 leads to increase in mGluR surface expression and mGluR-regulated AMPAR endocytic trafficking.
source: Together, these data indicate that dendritic loss of Homer1b/c caused by ablation of SNX6 leads to increase in mGluR surface expression and mGluR-regulated AMPAR endocytic trafficking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mGluR and AMPAR surface expression data.

claim: Ablation of SNX6 caused ~2 fold increase in the fraction of EZ (clathrin)-negative synapses.
source: To determine whether ablation of SNX6 caused uncoupling of the EZ from the PSD, we performed co-immunostaining of PSD95 and clathrin heavy chain, a marker for the EZ. Indeed, ablation of SNX6 caused ~2 fold increase in the fraction of EZ (clathrin)-negative synapses (Figure 9—figure supplement 4), indicating that the coupling of the EZ to the PSD is impaired in Snx6-/- neurons, which might also contribute to lower surface levels of AMPAR in dendritic spines.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 4.

claim: The coupling of the EZ to the PSD is impaired in Snx6-/- neurons, which might also contribute to lower surface levels of AMPAR in dendritic spines.
source: To determine whether ablation of SNX6 caused uncoupling of the EZ from the PSD, we performed co-immunostaining of PSD95 and clathrin heavy chain, a marker for the EZ. Indeed, ablation of SNX6 caused ~2 fold increase in the fraction of EZ (clathrin)-negative synapses (Figure 9—figure supplement 4), indicating that the coupling of the EZ to the PSD is impaired in Snx6-/- neurons, which might also contribute to lower surface levels of AMPAR in dendritic spines.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clathrin staining data.

claim: Depletion of VPS35 in mature neurons caused a decrease not only in surface GluA1 but also in the number of Homer1b/c puncta in dendrites.
source: Immunofluorescence staining and quantitative analysis of confocal images indicated that depletion of VPS35 in mature neurons caused a decrease not only in surface GluA1 but also in the number of Homer1b/c puncta in dendrites (Figure 10C–E), possibly resulted from reduced spine density as VPS35 has been found to promote spine formation and maturation (Tian et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 10C-E and citations to Tian et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2012.

claim: Compared with the phenotypes of Snx6-/- neurons, there was decrease in Homer1b/c signals throughout the cell body and dendrites, but no change in spine distribution of Homer1b/c or surface levels of mGluR5 when VPS35 was depleted.
source: Nevertheless, compared with the phenotypes of Snx6-/- neurons, there was decrease in Homer1b/c signals throughout the cell body and dendrites, but no change in spine distribution of Homer1b/c or surface levels of mGluR5 when VPS35 was depleted (Figure 10C and E–H), indicating that it serves distinct function(s) from SNX6 in dendritic distribution of postsynaptic proteins.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 10C and E-H.

claim: VPS35 serves distinct function(s) from SNX6 in dendritic distribution of postsynaptic proteins.
source: Nevertheless, compared with the phenotypes of Snx6-/- neurons, there was decrease in Homer1b/c signals throughout the cell body and dendrites, but no change in spine distribution of Homer1b/c or surface levels of mGluR5 when VPS35 was depleted (Figure 10C and E–H), indicating that it serves distinct function(s) from SNX6 in dendritic distribution of postsynaptic proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the VPS35 knockdown data.

claim: Live imaging of hippocampal neurons coexpressing mEmerald-Homer1c and VPS35-mCherry did not detect comovement of Homer1c- and VPS35-labeled vesicles in dendrite.
source: Moreover, live imaging of hippocampal neurons coexpressing mEmerald-Homer1c and VPS35-mCherry did not detect comovement of Homer1c- and VPS35-labeled vesicles in dendrite (Figure 10I,J and Videos 15 and 16).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 10I-J and Videos 15-16.

claim: Colocalization between Homer1b/c and VPS35 was very little compared with that between Homer1b/c and SNX6 or EEA1, and it was not affected by ablation of SNX6.
source: To further confirm that SNX6 does not cooperate with the retromer to regulate motility of Homer1b/c vesicles, we performed coimmunostaining of Homer1b/c and VPS35 on Snx6+/+ and Snx6-/- neurons. Quantitative analysis showed that colocalization between Homer1b/c and VPS35 was very little compared with that between Homer1b/c and SNX6 or EEA1. Moreover, it was not affected by ablation of SNX6 (Figure 10—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: No change in colocalization between Homer1b/c and SNX6 was detected in VPS35-depleted neurons.
source: Conversely, no change in colocalization between Homer1b/c and SNX6 was detected in VPS35-depleted neurons either (Figure 10—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: SNX6 functions independent of retromer to regulate dendritic distribution of Homer1b/c.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that SNX6 functions independent of retromer to regulate dendritic distribution of Homer1b/c.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the VPS35 knockdown and colocalization data.

claim: Ablation of SNX6 in the CNS causes deficits in spatial learning and memory, a hippocampal-dependent brain function.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that ablation of SNX6 in the CNS causes deficits in spatial learning and memory, a hippocampal-dependent brain function.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Loss of SNX6 causes a decrease in spine density in the distal apical dendrites of CA1 hippocampal cells and impairment of their AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission.
source: At the cellular level, loss of SNX6 causes a decrease in spine density in the distal apical dendrites of CA1 hippocampal cells and impairment of their AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission, indicating that SNX6 is required for synaptic structure and function of these excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: SNX6 is required for synaptic structure and function of CA1 excitatory neurons.
source: At the cellular level, loss of SNX6 causes a decrease in spine density in the distal apical dendrites of CA1 hippocampal cells and impairment of their AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission, indicating that SNX6 is required for synaptic structure and function of these excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cellular data.

claim: There is decrease in Homer1b/c distribution in distal dendrites in Snx6-/- neurons.
source: We also show that SNX6 directly interacts with Homer1b/c, a PSD scaffolding protein crucial for the structural and functional integrity of dendritic spines, and that there is decrease in Homer1b/c distribution in distal dendrites in Snx6-/- neurons.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: The spine density and surface AMPAR level phenotypes of Snx6-/- neurons could be rescued by overexpressing Homer1b/c or SNX6.
source: Moreover, the spine density and surface AMPAR level phenotypes of Snx6-/- neurons could be rescued by overexpressing Homer1b/c or SNX6.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: These findings reveal an important physiological function of SNX6 in the CNS excitatory neurons.
source: These findings reveal an important physiological function of SNX6 in the CNS excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the significance of the findings.
